item.title: Atmosphere of lava planet: ‘A cloudy, reflective sunscreen’ - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• The super-Earth exoplanet TOI-561 b is hot and its surface is likely covered by molten lava. An atmosphere for this lava planet was an unexpected discovery.
  • Additional observations using the Webb space telescope have re-confirmed the existence of this world’s dense atmosphere.
  • The new observations also show that the atmosphere of TOI-561 b is highly reflective, with clouds or haze.

The 2027 lunar calendar from EarthSky is now available! See the moon’s phase for every day of the year. Get yours now!

Surprising atmosphere of lava planet TOI-561 b re-confirmed by Webb

Last December, scientists at the Carnegie Institution for Science in Washington, D.C. said rocky exoplanet TOI-561 b was a scorching hot super-Earth — a lava planet — with a thick atmosphere. It was a surprise, because scientists had thought it was too small and too close to its star to hold an atmosphere.

TOI-561 b is located some 280.5 light-years from Earth, in the direction of our constellation Sextans. It orbits extremely near its host star, completing a single orbit (a full “year”) in under 10.5 hours. Surface temperatures are estimated to be over 2,000 K (around 3,100°F / 1,700°C). At these extreme temperatures, rock melts, creating a global ocean of molten lava on its dayside.

Now we have an update on this fascinating world. Some of the same researchers that conducted the earlier study — led this time by the University of Montreal in Canada — said on October 27, 2026, that they used the James Webb Space Telescope to re-observe TOI-561 b. Their observations showed that there are clouds or haze in the atmosphere of this world. They also suggest it reflects much of the heat coming from the planet’s star back into space.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed findings in The Astronomical Journal on September 29, 2026.

And Evan Gough wrote about the latest observations for Universe Today on October 27, 2026.

A surprising atmosphere

TOI-561 b is what scientists call an ultra-short period (USP) planet. Even though it is a super-Earth, scientists thought that it was too small — and hot — to hold on to any atmosphere, due to being so close to its star.

But it seems that TOI-561 b does have an atmosphere, and a thick one at that. The paper states:

Ultrashort period (USP) rocky planets are expected to be depleted of any substantial gaseous envelope due to the intense irradiation they receive from their host star, making the recent detection of an atmosphere around TOI-561 b particularly surprising. That finding was based on the planet’s bulk density and dayside emission spectrum, but full-orbit phase-curve observations offer a more comprehensive way to constrain the presence and characteristics of a planet’s atmosphere.

The atmosphere of the lava planet is highly reflective

The researchers used Webb to observe TOI-561 b for 37 hours. That worked out to seeing three orbits of the planet, at 10.5 hours per orbit. That is good, because the more orbits that can be observed, the better for gathering data.

The previous observations had also shown that TOI-561 b has an atmosphere. How did the researchers determine this?

The dayside of the planet was a lot cooler than expected. That shouldn’t be the case if the planet had no atmosphere.

There were two possible explanations. Either heat was being reflected back into space or the atmosphere transported it to the nightside. But the results showed the nightside wasn’t warm enough. The researchers estimated that about 3/4 of the planet’s heat must be reflected into space. The paper states:

We conclude from the GCM simulations that heat redistribution alone cannot match the observed dayside fluxes or amplitude of the phase curve, and a high-albedo source (Ab = 0.6) indicative of clouds or haze.

Co-author Lisa Dang is the project lead at the University of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada. She explained:

We measured how the planet’s brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.

Multiple kinds of clouds

The researchers said that clouds or haze are likely reflecting the heat. Silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium metasilicate (MgSiO3) are two of the most likely compositions of the clouds. The paper states that:

… multiple possible cloud species can form on the dayside, including MgSiO3 and SiO2.

Challenging current theories

The findings are surprising, and they also challenge current theories about rocky ultra-short period planets. Dang said:

Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago. Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today.

And the paper states:

Atmospheric-escape theory suggests that strongly irradiated super-Earths should be devoid of any volatile envelopes. This is particularly astonishing given that the current JWST census of rocky exoplanets has been interpreted as suggestive of a population of bare-rock planets …

It’s also notable that TOI-561 b orbits a sun-like star. Most ultra-short period planets orbit red dwarfs. And red dwarfs are known for their bursts of deadly radiation. That radiation can strip the atmospheres off planets that are too close.

Yet TOI-561 b receives more radiation from its star than typical red dwarfs. And it still has an atmosphere! How is that possible?

How is the atmosphere of lava planet TOI-561 b possible?

The researchers aren’t sure how TOI-561 b has been able to keep its atmosphere. But they have ideas.

It might have started out with an even much thicker primordial atmosphere, perhaps as a sub-Neptune (larger than a super-Earth). The radiation might have indeed stripped away most or all of that atmosphere. So what’s left now is a secondary atmosphere.

It’s also possible that the planet originated much farther out from its star than where it is now. That would be when the star was still young. At that time, it emitted even more radiation.

When the planet migrated closer to the star, the star was already “calming down” and emitting less radiation. As a result, the remaining atmosphere was spared from destruction.

Or it could be that the answer lies in both scenarios.

But there’s another possibility, too. The planet “consumed” its original atmosphere. In other words, the atmosphere became trapped in the interior of the planet.

Co-author Anjali Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said:

Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago. Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere.

Venus or Io?

The researchers want to know if TOI-561 b is more similar to Venus or Jupiter’s volcanic moon Io. Dang said:

The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b’s atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of lo. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with the JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years.

The unexpected atmosphere of lava world TOI-561 b was a big surprise to astronomers. But it will also provide valuable data for studying other rocky super-Earth planets. How many other also have atmospheres, and what kind?

Bottom line: More recent observations of hot super-Earth TOI-561 b by the Webb space telescope show again that the lava planet’s surprising atmosphere does exist. And it’s very reflective.

Source: A Highly Reflective Atmosphere on the Lava World TOI-561b Revealed by JWST/NIRSpec Phase Curves

item.title: Ghostly white animals: What’s the cause? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Color plays an outsized role in the animal kingdom. What scary things can happen when color production goes awry?

Animals use color to communicate in many ways. For example, some creatures camouflage themselves to hide from predators, like moths that look like tree bark (nothing to see here!). And animals can display warning colors that scream beware, like black and white striped skunks and red poison dart frogs.

Colors also can absorb light to keep animals warm, act as sunscreen, and communicate social status or readiness to breed. Some colors change over time, while others are permanent throughout an animal’s lifespan.

So how are colors made? What can happen when things go wrong? Here’s the science behind animal color, and how some animals end up ghostly white.

How are colors made?

Colors that appear in animal fur, feathers, and skin are largely the result of three primary mechanisms: genes, diet, and physics.

Genes. Genes code for the building blocks (amino acids) and enzymes (proteins) that produce the pigment melanin. A specific type of melanin called eumelanin creates the blacks, browns, and grays widely seen throughout the animal kingdom. Another type, called pheomelanin, makes those reddish-browns, oranges, and yellows, such as those found in orangutan hair and tiger stripes.

There are other types of endogenous (produced within) pigments too, like porphyrins pteridines, and psittacins. The latter are responsible for a parrot’s bright colors.

Diet. Many yellow, orange, and red colors in the animal kingdom are created by pigments called carotenoids. However, unlike melanin, animals cannot make carotenoids. Instead, animals acquire these plant-, algae-, or microbe-derived pigments through their diets. These are known as exogenous (produced without) pigments.

As example, the bright yellow colors of American goldfinch (Spinus tristis) come from the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin consumed in foods like asters, dandelions, sunflower hearts, and goldenrod.

Physics. Lastly, reflective physical structures can create an illusion of color. The brilliant blue feathers of bluejays (Cyanocitta cristata) are created by microscopic structures that scatter (randomly deflect) certain wavelengths of light. The color your eyes see is a result of the selective reflection of blue wavelengths of light. Red wavelengths get absorbed by the feathers.

Iridescent colors in the animal kingdom are another spectacular example of structural coloration. For example, iridescent throat feathers of hummingbirds, called the gorget, are created by structures that refract (bend) light.

Genetic mutations affecting color

Two genetic disorders that lead to a lack of color production in animals are leucism and albinism.

In leucistic animals, the cells that produce melanin — called melanocytes — don’t form, or don’t migrate properly to the intended destinations during embryonic development.

Without melanocytes, the overlying skin, fur, or feathers remain white. Eyes, however, are not affected. That is because melanin is produced differently in the eyes of embryos than in other parts of the body. Mutations in several different genes can cause leucism. The white areas may appear patchy if some parts of the body were not impacted.

In albino animals, melanocytes are present in proper locations, but the cells cannot produce melanin because of defective enzyme activity. Enzymes are specialized proteins that trigger or speed up biochemical reactions. In albinism, the enzyme tyrosinase is unable to make melanin.

In albino animals, the eyes are affected and appear as pink or red because of underlying blood vessels. Mutations in several different genes can cause albinism.

Genetic mutations can also lead to an overproduction of color. Such animals are termed melanistic. Visitors to Niagara Falls and surrounding regions are often treated to sightings of black squirrels. These are actually Eastern gray squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) that overproduce melanin.

Occasionally, a melanistic squirrel will appear sporting Halloween colors: a black body but bright orange tail. The black is eumelanin, while the orange is pheomelanin. Both pigments start from the same precursor, dopaquinone. How exactly the black and orange colors in the squirrel’s body and tail differentiate is a bit of a mystery to me. Please drop a comment if you know the mechanisms involved.

Why aren’t leucistic and albino animals more common?

Anecdotally, leucistic and albino animals are thought to be rare because they are noticeable and easy targets for predators. A few scientific studies do bear this out. However, context matters and there are other reasons why white animals might not survive long in the wild.

Albino animals have poor vision, and this deficit can contribute to their early demise. In an experiment with captive cane toads (Rhinella marina), Alexander Funk and colleagues used CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to knock out the gene for the enzyme that makes melanin. They then raised the white tadpoles and frogs along with pigmented ones in aquaria without predators. The white tadpoles were less successful at foraging for food because of their poor vision, and they showed lower rates of survival.

Additionally, albino animals may be more susceptible to skin cancer and have trouble regulating body temperature. In birds, the feathers lacking pigment are weaker.

Images of ghostly white animals tend to attract a lot of attention on social media. Like this sighting: Rare white killer whale caught on camera. Next time you see such a post, help explain why the animal looks that way.

Bottom line: Atypical white animals may be leucistic or albino due to genetic mutations that disrupt color production.

item.title: Could the Taurid meteors bring a risk of airbursts in 2026? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Could Taurid meteors bring an airburst in 2026?

Last year, we told you about a new study suggesting the yearly Taurid meteor shower — and its associated Halloween fireballs — might bring an increased risk of an airburst in 2032 and 2036. The lead author of that study, physicist and planetary defense expert Mark Boslough of the University of New Mexico, contacted EarthSky this week.

His new calculations now suggest a risk of airburst from the Taurids in 2026. But he says the possibility rests on two big, unproven assumptions. Let’s dive in.

In the 2025 study, researchers described a hypothetical swarm of larger objects within the Taurid meteor stream. The study suggested Earth could pass near this swarm in 2032 and 2036, potentially increasing the risk of an airburst in our atmosphere. What’s an airburst? It’s an explosion in Earth’s atmosphere caused by an incoming space rock. The most famous airburst happened in the Tunguska region of Siberia in 1908. And the Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013 — which broke windows in six Russian cities — was also an airburst.

Boslough has now outlined a more speculative possibility: Could more Taurid objects — related to the famous 1908 Tunguska explosion — still be out there in space? And if so, could they return to Earth’s vicinity in 2026?

Tunguska and the Taurids

The Tunguska event flattened forestland in Siberia. Scientists say it happened when a space rock created an airburst in the atmosphere. And some researchers have linked the Tunguska event to the Beta Taurids, a daytime meteor shower associated with the same stream of debris that produces the better-known North and South Taurids in October and November.

Boslough’s 2025 study related to hypothetical objects — associated with the Taurid meteor stream — that might be in an resonance orbit with Earth. An orbital resonance is two orbiting bodies whose orbital periods are related by some ratio.

In other words, was the object that created the Tunguska event a solitary object in space? Or was it part of a cluster of objects, which in turn are associated with the well-known Taurid meteor shower? And if so are there still objects out there in space in a resonance orbit with Earth — an orbit that will bring them back to our vicinity?

We don’t know the answers to these questions. But Boslough estimates that — if they exist — such objects would orbit the sun 18 times for every 61 Earth orbits (an 18:61 resonance orbit with Earth).

So if the Tunguska object did belong to a cluster of debris in that particular resonance orbit, then the cluster — perhaps containing objects big enough to create another airburst — might return to Earth’s vicinity every 61 years. 1908 + 61 = 1969. And 1969 + 61 = 2030. So what does that mean for 2026?

Mark Boslough told EarthSky that, yes, an object in a 61-year resonance orbit would return in June 1930. But, he said:

So imagine if the Tunguska object had missed the Earth in 1908. Then it could return in 2030.  The Halloween 2026 date is significant because the same resonance that creates a close June encounter in 2030 creates a close encounter around Halloween, four years earlier (2026). 

…The good thing about the Taurid resonant swarm hypothesis is that it’s testable. And we will know for sure in 2032 if it really exists.

Of course, these are all events based on hypotheticals. As Boslough told EarthSky, this might only happen:

…IF the Tunguska object was part of a cluster, and IF it had the same orbital elements as the hypothetical swarm (both are big ifs). I will be the first to caution that this is highly speculative because of those two big IFs. We do not know if either are true.

Read on for more insight from the 2025 study.

Halloween fireballs

The term Halloween fireballs refers to the unusually bright meteors (fireballs) produced in some years (but not all years) by the Taurid meteor shower. This shower peaks every year in late October and early November. So if you’re a meteor watcher, there’s a good chance you’ve seen a Halloween fireball already.

Most meteor showers come from comets. When a comet comes in toward the sun, it warms up and releases a trail of debris – dust particles and rocks – along its path. Earth frequently crosses comet paths in its own orbit around the sun. The bits of comet dust and rock enter our atmosphere and burn up due to friction with the air … and voila! We have a meteor shower.

The Taurid shower is a bit different. Astronomers believe it might be the result of a large object that broke up, creating Comet Encke and several asteroids. And scientists think that one of those asteroids – 2004 TG10 – is the parent to the Taurid meteor shower. This asteroid, which the Spacewatch program discovered on October 8, 2004, has an orbit that matches Comet Encke.

And there are multiple Taurid meteor showers. The South and North Taurids are November meteor showers, and the Beta Taurids in June are a daylight shower. They are all associated with Comet Encke and its debris.

Do the Taurid fireballs suggest larger-sized objects moving within the Taurid meteor stream? Some astronomers have even suggested there could be large asteroids hiding in the Taurid stream. But we don’t know if that’s the case.

A matter of planetary defense

Still, it’s a possibility we have to take seriously. Astronomer Mark Boslough said that investigating the possibility of the Taurid meteors producing airbursts is a matter of planetary defense. That’s because, in the past, airbursts have wreaked havoc on the ground.

Boslough said:

Planetary defense is the multidisciplinary and internationally coordinated effort to protect the Earth and its inhabitants from impacts by near-Earth objects. It requires surveys to discover and track near-Earth objects, campaigns to characterize those that are hazardous, modeling efforts to understand and predict impact effects and associated consequences, and mitigation through impact avoidance and/or civil defense.

Researching the Halloween fireballs

The researchers looked at observational data on the Taurid meteors. They found:

… the risk from airburst-sized near-Earth objects, which are small enough to explode in the atmosphere instead of striking the ground, might be larger than currently estimated.

The debris that lights up the Taurid meteors or Halloween fireballs is in harmony with Jupiter’s orbit. For every seven orbits of the sun the debris stream makes, Jupiter makes two orbits. This puts it in resonance with Jupiter. So part of its stream approaches Jupiter at regular intervals. And Jupiter’s large gravity might help organize that stream into dense clusters. The researchers said if Jupiter is indeed having this affect on the swarm, Earth could pass near these denser clusters in 2032 and 2036.

Thus we have the increased risk of airbursts in Earth’s atmosphere.

Bottom line: A researcher from the University of New Mexico said the Taurid meteor shower could bring an increased risk of an airburst in 2026. But it’s based on some pretty big IFs.

item.title: Is this our solar system’s future? Scientists spot disk around dead star - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Is this our solar system’s future?

About 5 billion years from now, the sun will near the end of its life when it uses up its supply of hydrogen. Then it will temporarily expand into a red giant for about 1 billion years. Finally, it will blow off its outer layers in a last gasp. All that will be left behind is the sun’s dense, dead core: a white dwarf. But what about the planets circling the sun? What will happen to them? What is our solar system’s future?

Scientists from the European Southern Observatory said on October 27, 2026, that they’ve spotted a white dwarf star with a debris disk circling it. This could be a glimpse at what the solar system’s future holds.

The disk consists of two rings that circle the white dwarf at different speeds. The scientists think the two rings were shaped by two planetary bodies that partially survived the star’s violent transformation. One of the surviving worlds could be as large as Pluto, or even our moon.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed study in the journal Nature Astronomy on October 26, 2026.

A white dwarf star with separate disks

The researchers used the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope in Chile to study the white dwarf, named J1328-1450. Other studies have found a disk around white dwarf stars before. But this is the first time researchers have spotted a disk with a distinct gap separating it into two parts. Lead author Nicola Gentille Fusillo at the University of Trieste in Italy said:

We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disk and potentially two surviving planetesimals.

Co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches of the University of Warwick in the U.K. and the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile added:

The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap.

Gentile Fusillo remarked:

The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disk structures far more complex than previously realized.

Hence, a foreshadowing of our solar system’s future a few billion years from now.

2 possible surviving planetary remnants

The researchers said the most likely scenario that resulted in the two rings is that they came from two planet-like bodies that partly survived in their separate orbits. They said the inner object could be about the size of an asteroid, approximately a mile or more across. Meanwhile, the outer object could be larger, the size of Pluto or Earth’s moon.

Although they have not spotted the bodies themselves, the researchers have detected elements in the disk, such as calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron. And the composition of each of those rings is different. The inner ring is rich in magnesium gas while the outer ring has little. This could bolster the idea of the rings being from two planets with different compositions.

However, there is still the possibility that the debris in the rings was from one planet, with one ring getting material from the crust and the other ring fed by the core of a planet.

Bottom line: Researchers have discovered a dead star — a white dwarf — surrounded by a debris disk with two separate rings. It offers a glimpse at what the solar system’s future might look like.

item.title: The enormous oarfish could inspire new ways to explore the ocean - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
The giant oarfish

If you’re fascinated by extraordinary creatures like the Loch Ness Monster, get ready to meet a real-life giant. But forget about the Scottish lochs. The oarfish inhabits the ocean’s depths, a dark world where sunlight barely reaches.

Few people have been lucky enough to see this magnificent animal in its vast natural habitat. And even fewer have had the chance to study it in depth. But late last month, a team of scientists discovered something fascinating. They unlocked the intricate mechanics behind this creature’s movement.

Could the oarfish’s remarkably efficient and stealthy swimming, powered by its long dorsal fin, hold the key to new advances in underwater robotics? Scientists hope these nature-inspired innovations could one day let us explore the ocean’s hidden wonders while leaving its inhabitants undisturbed.

The researchers published their study in the peer-reviewed journal BioOne on September 30, 2026.

The oarfish’s fin inspires underwater robotics

The giant oarfish can reach around 26 feet (8 meters) in length, making it a true ocean colossus. Its body is long and slender, with a ribbon-like shape that gradually tapers toward the rear. Just to give you an idea of how enormous it is, it took no fewer than 15 people to hold a specimen measuring 23 feet (7 meters)!

And its appearance is just as striking. This creature has no scales; instead, its sides shimmer with a brilliant silvery sheen thanks to a covering that contains guanine.

This smooth, metallic surface contrasts with its vivid red and orange dorsal fin. The fin runs along almost the entire length of its back. The first few fin rays are especially long, forming a striking crest above its head, as if the fish were wearing a crown of fire.

But its long dorsal fin is far more than decoration. It plays a major role in the fish’s movement. It generates waves along the fin without requiring large side-to-side movements of the body.

This raises a fascinating question: how does the fish coordinate such a long structure, made up of numerous fin rays, to produce such fluid motion? To understand this, researchers must look beyond its striking silhouette. They must examine how the muscles, joints and skeletal elements of its fin are arranged.

This is where a research project begins to connect the biology of the fish with a very different field: underwater robotics.

The oarfish: Inspired by nature, designed to explore

Unlike many fish, the oarfish propels itself by sending waves along its dorsal fin while keeping its body relatively steady. Scientists already knew it swam this way. But they still needed to understand how it controls such a long, complex structure with such precise coordination.

To investigate, a research team led by Gabriel Vinícius Felix Afonso, a Ph.D. student at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, studied the anatomy of the dorsal fin in detail. They examined specimens, using imaging techniques and analyzing videos of oarfish in the wild. They studied how the muscles, joints and fin rays are arranged and how they work together to produce movement.

The findings revealed a surprising mechanism: a group of six muscles controls each fin ray, which attach to it at 12 points. The joint also works much like a ball-and-socket joint, similar to the one in the human shoulder, allowing it to rotate in every direction through a full 360 degrees. Together, these muscles and joints help explain how the fish coordinates its fin movements to generate waves along its length.

Where does the name oarfish come from?

Interestingly, the oarfish’s name does not come from its striking dorsal fin, but from its unusually long pelvic fins. Located beneath the front part of its body, each of these fins consists of a single ray that resembles a little oar. But despite inspiring the fish’s name, these pelvic fins are not primarily responsible for its distinctive swimming motion. That role belongs to the dorsal fin, whose precisely coordinated movements allow waves to travel along the fish’s body.

We asked Felix Afonso about why the oarfish inspired him to think about aquatic robotics. He said:

If you look at large species of fish that live in the open ocean, you will see fish with spindle-like shapes, such as tunas and billfish, as well as round shapes, such as sunfish and opahs. Unlike those species, the oarfish has an unusual body shape for an open-ocean fish. Interestingly, the oarfish does not swim by undulating its body like an eel. Instead, the oarfish keeps its body rigid while only its long dorsal fin undulates. This combination of an unusual body shape and an unexpected swimming mode attracted our attention, prompting us to study the oarfish’s functional morphology for future biomimetic robotic applications.

An inhabitant of the deep

Despite its unforgettable size, shimmering appearance, super-long pelvic fins and hypnotic dorsal fin motion, the oarfish remains one of the lesser-known inhabitants of the deep ocean.

The oarfish is found throughout the world’s oceans, particularly in tropical and temperate waters. But it lives mainly in open water, far from shore and at depths where sunlight grows increasingly faint.

It is typically found hundreds of feet below the surface, with records reaching depths of around 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). There, in an environment that is difficult to observe directly, much of its life unfolds beyond our view, leaving researchers with many unanswered questions.

In addition, sightings near the surface are unusual and sometimes involve animals that are weakened or in distress. This makes their behavior difficult to study. Finding a stranded specimen or one close to shore allows scientists to examine its anatomy, but it is not the same as observing how it lives and behaves in its natural environment.

A giant that feeds on tiny prey

You might expect an animal this size to feed like a formidable predator, but the reality is quite different. The oarfish feeds mainly on small organisms, including krill and other planktonic crustaceans. Small fish and squid have also been reported among its possible prey.

Its head is relatively small compared with the length of its body and ends in a short, protrusible mouth that can extend forward to capture food. But it doesn’t need powerful jaws or an impressive set of teeth: its gill structures help trap tiny organisms as water passes through its mouth. Rather than chasing large prey, it makes use of much smaller food sources suspended in the water.

It’s remarkable that a fish capable of growing many feet long gets much of its nourishment from such tiny creatures. It’s also a reminder of just how diverse feeding strategies can be among marine animals.

The oarfish has also been observed swimming vertically, with its head pointing upward. Scientists believe this posture may help it spot prey silhouetted against the light filtering down from the surface. It may also make the fish less visible to predators looking down from above.

Nature’s lessons for safe ocean exploration

Over millions of years, animals have evolved remarkable ways to move, feed and adapt to their surroundings. Studying these abilities allows us to better understand the natural world, revealing just how much there is still to learn from the creatures with which we share our planet.

What we learn from them can also inspire new technologies. In the case of the oarfish, understanding how it swims could help researchers develop quieter underwater robots, opening up new ways to explore the ocean and observe marine life while causing as little disturbance as possible.

The more we learn about animals and the environments they depend on, the better we can protect them. By combining scientific discovery with more respectful ways of exploring, we can uncover some of the ocean’s secrets while helping preserve the remarkable life it sustains.

Bottom line: The giant oarfish has a remarkable fin that could inspire quieter underwater robots and open new possibilities for ocean exploration and conservation.

item.title: Origins of Uranus and Neptune are surprisingly different - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Uranus and Neptune seem to be quite similar. But are the origins of Uranus and Neptune the same?
  • The origins of the two planets are quite different, according to a new study from an international team of researchers.
  • They say Uranus formed where it is located today, but Neptune’s building blocks first formed much closer to the sun.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

The origins of Uranus and Neptune

Uranus and Neptune appear to be much alike, and in some ways they are. But a new study from an international team of scientists says that the origins of Uranus and Neptune are quite different.

The researchers said on October 19, 2026, that Neptune’s material building blocks originated much closer to the sun than those of Uranus. So although the two planets are superficially similar, their evolutionary paths are quite different.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed results in Astronomy & Astrophysics on October 19, 2026.

Planetary twins … or not?

Uranus and Neptune have long been regarded as “twins.” They’re similar in size, both blue or greenish-blue, with deep atmospheres of methane, ammonia and water. There are no solid surfaces beneath their atmospheres. Co-author Olivier Mousis, a program director in the Southwest Research Institute’s (SwRI’s) Solar System Science and Exploration Division in Boulder, Colorado, said:

Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories. Their atmospheric compositions may be connected to different regions of the protoplanetary disk where the planets formed, which would make their similarities a noteworthy coincidence.

Similar worlds, different origins

Despite their seeming similarities, the new study suggests that the origins of Uranus and Neptune are rather different. The researchers made this determination by studying their atmospheres. This included new measurements from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the Atacama Desert in Chile.

Interestingly, Neptune’s atmosphere has more oxygen than Uranus’. This creates a different carbon-oxygen ratio. The researchers used models to compare this to the dust and gases in the protoplanetary disk billions of years ago. That is, the disk of dust and gas around the young sun where the planets were born. As Mousis explained:

We can’t directly access the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, but chemical tracers allow us to probe the conditions hidden beneath their visible clouds. Studying carbon monoxide, or CO, is particularly useful because of its abundance in many planets’ upper troposphere. Using this data, we can model the chemical evolution of the protoplanetary disk and the origins of its materials.

Migrating outward from the sun

The most surprising finding is that the building blocks of Neptune first formed much closer to the sun. This is because volatile compounds — ones that can evaporate easily — condensed into solids at different distances from the young sun.

This created distinct chemical reservoirs of material at various distances. The new research models showed that the material that formed Neptune was originally a lot closer to the sun than it is now. As a result, the origins of Uranus and Neptune diverged.

Later, over time, that material migrated outward. It eventually reached the region where Neptune is today. Mousis said:

Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus. Instead, our models lead us to believe that its building blocks traveled a long way to where Neptune could accrete them. In short, two superficially similar worlds may have reached their present locations and formations through two very distinct evolutionary paths.

Limited understanding of the atmospheres

The new findings are compelling, but the researchers acknowledge that they are limited. This is because we currently can’t study the planets’ atmospheres in situ, with a spacecraft.

The findings also have implications for similar kinds of planets much farther away. Mousis said:

Our findings have implications beyond Neptune and Uranus and even far beyond our solar system. Similarly sized planets are common around other stars, which is why Uranus and Neptune are essential benchmarks for understanding how planets form and evolve throughout the galaxy. This is precisely why missions like NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe, expected to launch sometime in the next decade, are so important.

The true colors of Uranus and Neptune

In 2024, researchers at the University of Oxford in the U.K. said that they had determined the real colors of Uranus and Neptune. Uranus had always looked light greenish-blue, while Neptune was a much darker azure blue.

But their study showed that Neptune wasn’t actually as dark as previously thought. It was a lighter greenish-blue, more similar to Uranus.

And at the beginning of this year, researchers from the University of Zurich and NCCR PlanetS in Switzerland said that Uranus and Neptune might be rocky worlds deep inside … Not ice giants as long thought. Interesting!

Bottom line: A new study suggests that the origins of Uranus and Neptune are quite different, even though the two planets are similar in many ways.

Source: Contrasting C/O ratios in Uranus and Neptune from disequilibrium chemistry: A clue to distinct evolutionary pathways?

Via SwRI

item.title: A Deep-Mantle Garnet Might Hold the Secret to Ancient Martian Magma - Universe Today
item.description: A history of a planet’s volcanic activity is contained in its rocks. And Mars’ rocks - or at least many of the meteorites that have made the journey from it to Earth - were telling a contradictory story. They appeared to be highly oxidized, but our understanding of the internal volcanic forces on Mars meant that they should have been formed in a reducing environment - the exact opposite of what the chemical makeup of the rocks themselves indicate. Now, a new paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth from planetary scientists Hideharu Kuwahara and Ryoichi Nakada of Ehime University provides an answer as to why - and it involves a gemstone.

item.title: Lacerta the Lizard, home to a blazar - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Finding the constellation Lacerta the Lizard

Lacerta the Lizard is a small, faint constellation in the northern sky. It’s best seen on autumn evenings, when it climbs high above the horizon. But this unassuming patch of sky holds something extraordinary: BL Lacertae, a blazar powered by a supermassive black hole in a distant galaxy. One of its powerful jets points nearly toward us, making it appear unusually bright, giving astronomers a powerful way to study the black hole’s activity.

BL Lacertae looks like a faint, variable star, but it’s actually the bright center of an active galaxy. Its brightness changes over time, and astronomers have named an entire class of objects after it: BL Lacertae objects.

Lacerta isn’t an ancient constellation. Astronomer Johannes Hevelius created it in the late 1600s. Its name means lizard in Latin.

Do you know how to spot the Great Square of Pegasus the Flying Horse, the W-shaped Cassiopeia the Queen, the house-shaped Cepheus the King, or Cygnus the Swan? If you do, you can find Lacerta in the dark patch of sky surrounded by these four constellations.

Some people refer to Lacerta as the “little W,” due to its shape. The “big W” is, of course, Cassiopeia. Can you see the Big and Little Ws next to each other in the sky? Others see Lacerta in the shape of a skinny kite. Perhaps you can spot the form of a lizard among its stars.

Lacerta is a fairly small constellation, only taking up 200 square degrees in size. It’s the 68th largest of the 88 constellations.

The stars of the Lizard

Only one star within the constellation’s borders is brighter than magnitude 4: Alpha Lacertae at -3.76.

Lacerta now has several officially named stars. Its brightest star, Alpha Lacertae, received the name Stellio in 2024. Alpha Lacertae lies 102 light-years away.

To find Alpha Lacertae, start with Cassiopeia, the W- or M-shaped constellation. Then look toward Cygnus the Swan. Between them is Lacerta the Lizard. Use the star chart below to pinpoint Alpha Lacertae, but you will need to get away from bright streetlights to see the faint, little lizard shape!

Stars of 4th magnitude lie on all sides of Alpha Lacertae. The star in the direction of Polaris from Alpha Lacertae is Beta Lacertae. Beta Lacertae is another star in the constellation identified by a Greek letter. It has a magnitude of 4.42 and lies 170 light-years away.

Star clusters in Lacerta

The majority of the constellation Lacerta lies within the swath of the Milky Way. Yet, there are no Messier objects within it. The brightest star cluster in Lacerta is NGC 7243, which lies 2.5 degrees from Alpha Lacertae in the direction of Cygnus. NGC 7243 is magnitude 6.4, meaning that you can spot it in a pair of binoculars. It lies about 2,800 light-years away and displays some large foreground stars juxtaposed over the hazy Milky Way.

The next brightest cluster lies on the border of Cygnus and Lacerta. This cluster, NGC 7209, is magnitude 6.7 and has the nickname the Star Lizard Cluster. This loose, spread-out cluster lies a similar distance from Earth as NGC 7243.

Draw a line from Alpha through Beta Lacertae and extend it for an equal distance as Alpha and Beta are apart. You will arrive at two star clusters, NGC 7245 and IC 1442. IC 1442 is 9th magnitude and NGC 7245 is magnitude 9.19. So they are best viewed through a telescope. This pair lies only 20 arcminutes apart.

Exoplanet in Lacerta the Lizard

Several stars in Lacerta are known to host exoplanets.

One example is HD 213472 b, a gas giant discovered in 2021. The planet has about 3.5 times Jupiter’s mass and orbits its star at an average distance of approximately 13 astronomical units (AU). It takes about 46.6 Earth years to complete one orbit. The exoplanet and its star lie 210 light-years from Earth.

Don’t miss the next unmissable night sky event. Sign up to EarthSky’s free newsletter for daily night sky updates.

Bottom line: Lacerta the Lizard is a small, dim constellation in the fall sky that contains a blazar, an active galactic nucleus with a jet aimed toward Earth.

item.description:
The north-western sky as seen from Brisbane at 9:59 AEST on Tuesday 3 November. The moon is obvious above the horizon, but you will need binoculars or a telescope to see Jupiter.  The left-hand inset shows the magnified view just as the occultation starts, and the right-hand view is the view as Jupiter comes out from behind the Moon. The north-western sky as seen from Adelaide at 9:50 ACDST on Tuesday 3 November. The moon is obvious above the horizon, but you will need binoculars or a telescope to see Jupiter.  The left-hand inset shows the magnified view just as the occultation starts, and the right-hand view is the view as Jupiter comes out from behind the Moon. The northern sky as seen from Perth at 6:46 AWST on Tuesday 3 November. The moon is obvious above the horizon, but you will need binoculars or a telescope to see Jupiter.  The left-hand inset shows the magnified view just as the occultation starts, and the right-hand view is the view as Jupiter comes out from behind the Moon. 


WARNING! This daytime occultation occurs not far from the Sun and should be attempted by experienced observers only. The Moon will be 76 degrees (around 12 hand-spans) from the Sun. Exposure to the Sun through a telescope eye-piece can result in instant blindness. Any observation should be carried out with the sun blocked from view by a building or similar large, obscuring object with no possibility of the sun being accidentally observed.

On the morning of Tuesday 3 November Jupiter is occulted by waning Moon as seen from the most of Australia, Indonesia, Papua new Guinea  and New Zealand. However far north Queensland misses out. The Moon is just past last quarter and high in the north to northwest. It is an obvious signpost for where to look.  Jupiter will not be visible to the unaided eye, but in binoculars and telescopes Jupiter will be obvious close to the Moon. The times of disappearance and reappearance of Jupiter is in the table below. 

Most of Australia sees Jupiter's satellite Europa get occulted first, then Jupiter will take around 2 minutes to disappear behind the Moon. For Darwin and  Brisbane Jupiter will skim along the Moons surface as it exits from occultation. Caloundra sees the Moon graze Jupiter, every where in QLD above Caloundra on the coast and Cape York sees a very close approach, well worth watching.  

Telescopic view of Jupiter and its satellites just before the occultation. Europa leads the way. Telescopic view of Jupiter and its satellites just after the occultation. Europa still leads the way and the other satellites will appear to "pop" out.


Start watching about half an hour before hand to get set up and familiar with the sky. This is a daytime occultation requiring a small telescope or binoculars and extreme caution and attention to Sun safety. 

My blog of the 2012 Daylight Jupiter Moon graze should give you a feel for what it will look like, and some photography hints. 

Jupiter and its satellites will appear to "wink out" as it goes behind the bright limb of the Moon, reappearance will be harder to see as you have to be looking just at the right moment.

The occultation occurs in the early morning with the Moon reasonably high above the north-western to northern horizon. The Moon just past last quarter and should be obvious, but you will still need extreme care with the sun. 

The Moon is a signpost to Jupiter which will only be visible in binoculars or telescopes. It is advisable to set up and practice on the Moon in the morning before the event, so you are familiar with your telescope set-up. Set up at least half an hour ahead of time so that you can be sure everything is working well and you can watch the entire event comfortably (trying to focus your telescope moments before the occultation will cause a lot of unnecessary stress). Jupiter will be clearly visible in a telescope or binoculars near the Moon. Again, the Sun will be close by, so only experienced observers who can block out the Sun should attempt this.

item.description: The Earth’s magnetic field is responsible for shielding us from harmful space weather, including solar radiation from the Sun but also cosmic rays originating from outside our solar system. Cosmic rays can include deep space supernovas, so the magnetic field takes the majority of the brunt from solar radiation. Without our magnetic field, the solar wind would slowly strip away our atmosphere, making life on our small, blue world impossible to exist. But where is the magnetic field doing the heaviest lifting regarding how it filters out incoming space radiation?

item.description: Unlike the Moon, the Sun is constantly rotating from our perspective - but we still only see half of it at any given time. item.description: The magnetic environment around the Sun is a jumbled mess of chaotic fields and streams of charged particles. Recently we’ve been getting at least slightly better at mapping out its complexity, thanks in large part to data collected by missions like the Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter. But there’s still a large grey area surrounding the interface between the large scale hydrodynamic properties of plasmas and the microscopic properties of individual ions, and scientists believe understanding large scale features of the Sun, such as why its corona is so much hotter than its surface, may rely on our knowledge of that interface. A new paper that directly tackles some of the outstanding questions about that interface was recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by Masatomi Iizawa of the Technical University of Braunschweig and his co-authors.

item.title: Habitable worlds: Better than Earth? Scientists wonder - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Astronomers use the word habitable to mean a planet whose physical conditions might allow life – any form of life, perhaps microbial life – to exist there. 
  • Are there worlds more habitable than Earth? Some scientists think so.
  • They wonder if super-Earth planets — larger and more massive than Earth — might be better suited for life than Earth is.

Are there worlds more habitable than Earth?

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Scientists are seeking signs of life elsewhere in the universe. Even the tiniest microbe would be big news! So far, we don’t have conclusive evidence of any form of life on any planet beyond our own. So Earth is our primary model for what might be possible. Our planet is still the only one known to be brimming with life.

We know many rocky planets like Earth exist. Some are larger and more massive than Earth. We call them super-Earths. And we know that some are potentially habitable. Could they be even more habitable than Earth?

Some scientists have been weighing that idea. Nowadays, they are more confident than in past that such worlds might exist, especially since about 2010. The Kepler Space Telescope launched in 2009, for example. It has demonstrated that Earth-sized and super-Earth-sized planets are extremely common across our Milky Way galaxy.

Do the most habitable worlds orbit K dwarfs?

Beginning around 2010, astrobiologists — scientists who study the possibility of life beyond Earth — began recognizing that G-type stars like our sun might not be the best places for life. Research around this time highlighted orange dwarfs (K-type stars). They are far more abundant, have significantly longer lifespans (tens of billions of years in contrast to our sun’s 10 billion years) and emit less harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Around that time, scientists like René Heller and John Armstrong began challenging the anthropocentric assumption that an Earth twin is the ideal place for life. They formulated the concept of superhabitable worlds—super-Earths with stronger magnetic fields, thicker atmospheres, and warmer, more stable climates capable of supporting richer, more diverse ecosystems than Earth.

They teamed up in 2014 to present the hypothesis that smaller, cooler stars might be better for habitable planets. Why? Because they burn through their hydrogen fuel more slowly and brighten more gradually as they age. So they have longer lifespans for life to develop.

Our own sun only has about five billion years left before it turns into a red giant star. But K-type stars can live for 10s of billions of years. What kind of life could develop on planets in that length of time?

Armstrong, a professor at Weber State University in Utah, recently asked in the comments section of an astrobiology seminar on YouTube:

Shouldn’t there be planets more habitable than Earth?

What would these worlds be like?

Natalie Wolchover wrote about the fascinating possibility of superhabitable worlds for The New York Times on October 13, 2026. She pointed out that carbon-based life — like on Earth — could last longer and be even more diverse on such worlds than on Earth. But what might these planets be like?

The researchers say that typically they would be 20-30% larger than Earth and twice as massive. Hence, a super-Earth. Like Earth, they’d need water. But such massive rocky planets would have stronger gravity than Earth. They’d have been able to hold on to the ingredients for water as they formed. So they might have thicker atmospheres than Earth. They might have warmer and more stable climates.

Plus, super-Earths likely have iron cores that are larger than Earth’s. Those cores could produce stronger magnetic fields that would protect life even better than Earth’s magnetic field.

But — in the space of our Milky Way galaxy — do we know of any super-Earths orbiting more benign K-type stars better suited for life than Earth? The answer to that is no.

Experiments related to super-Earths

As noted in Wolchover’s article, astrobiologist Iva Vilovic at the Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics in Potsdam, Germany, thinks that life could thrive on super-Earths orbiting K-type stars.

She did experiments with garden cress. She simulated the light coming from a K-type star to see if photosynthesis would occur. And surprise! The plants grew even better than they did under regular sunlight on Earth. She told Wolchover:

K-dwarf light is a very, very interesting light source, and it should be considered, if not prioritized, for any type of search for extraterrestrial life, in my opinion.

The idea of a planet even more biologically diverse than Earth might be hard to imagine. On Earth, the tropics are some of the most biodiverse areas on the planet. But what if an entire planet was like that?

Consider that the light from the K-type star could reach to the bottom of a shallow ocean. This could help fuel an amazingly diverse marine ecosystem, including on any islands that might exist.

Is Earth only marginally habitable?

The seemingly endless kinds of life on Earth are breathtaking. But many scientists consider Earth to be only marginally habitable. If our planet were just 2% closer to the sun, for example, it probably wouldn’t have as much — if any — surface water.

So did we just get lucky?

René Heller, at the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research in Germany, thinks that maybe we shouldn’t be so focused on finding Earth’s “twin.” He said:

It occurred to me that currently, humanity is looking for Earthlike planets with the same anthropocentric bias. Of course, Earth is special to us. But from a universal perspective, why should Earth be a reference?

He also wonders about there being “someone to talk to,” saying:

Although I am not, at least in my everyday life, a very spiritual person, it’s nevertheless something that at least drives me, this question. Could there be someone?

How can we find worlds more habitable than Earth?

If such worlds do exist, how can we find them? The European Space Agency’s Plato mission is launching in 2027. The space telescope will be able to find potentially habitable planets, including super-Earths orbiting K-type stars. But it will have its limits. Heller said:

We will probably find a few of them, maybe a dozen. But we won’t learn much about them.

But there’s also the James Webb Space Telescope and the Extremely Large Telescope in Chile. Both can find potentially habitable super-Earths. And NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory — expected to launch sometime in the 2040s — will be able to make more detailed observations.

item.title: Is the Mars Grand Canyon still tectonically active? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Is the Mars Grand Canyon still tectonically active? Scientists say yes

Mars might be smaller than Earth, but its landscape features are overachievers. The red planet is home to both the largest volcano (Olympus Mons) and the largest canyon system (Valles Marineris) in the solar system. Valles Marineris is dubbed the Grand Canyon of Mars. It stretches more than 2,500 miles (4,000 km) long, nine times longer than the Grand Canyon on Earth. It’s also about 20 times wider and five times deeper than Earth’s Grand Canyon. On October 19, 2026, scientists with Columbia University and Imperial College London said Valles Marineris is still tectonically active, billions of years after it formed.

NASA’s InSight lander recently captured seismic data of a marsquake. The new research found the quake occurred 12 to 25 miles (20 to 40 km) beneath Valles Marineris. Rocks slipping along a fault deep in the red planet’s crust triggered the quake. But Mars does not have tectonic plates sliding around on the surface like Earth does. So the quakes today are happening along ancient fault lines on Mars.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed findings in the journal Nature Communications on October 15, 2026.

Science news, the night sky and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Tectonics on Mars versus Earth

Earth’s shaking, rattling and rolling is thanks to the tectonic plates that slide around on the upper mantle. The plates push, pull and slide against each other. Sometimes they get stuck and friction builds up. Eventually the stress snaps in an earthquake.

But quakes on Mars are different. Scientists describe Mars’ crust as similar to an outer shell that behaves like a single, slowly cooling lid. As Mars continues to cool from its early years, the crust shrinks and cracks. This activity forms faults that slip and cause seismic rumbles. And some of these faults, formed billions of years ago, can still slip and shift.

Finding a recent marsquake

On August 25, 2021, the InSight lander detected a quake from its location in Elysium Planitia, on the opposite side of Mars from Valles Marineris. At first, researchers didn’t know if the seismic activity was from a quake. That’s because tremors on Mars can also be from landslides or meteorite impacts.

But then researchers found the quake, named S0976a, had traveled through Mars’ core. Its epicenter was somewhere in the western Valles Marineris region. But its exact location and cause remained obscure.

The new research pinpoints the epicenter at 12 to 25 miles (20 to 40 km) beneath Valles Marineris. The researchers have now been able to learn about not just Mars’ core, but the trigger for the quake. Co-author Doyeon Kim of Imperial College London said:

S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event, playing an important role in our understanding of the red planet.

Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes.

Grand Canyon of Mars: home to ancient fault and modern stress

The team was able to analyze the seismic waves, including their amplitudes and direction. Then they could reconstruct what must have happened to cause the quake. They said a strike-slip marsquake event was the most likely cause. This happens when two chunks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep fault with a deep root. In this case, the quake was miles below ground. It created what would be equal to a magnitude 5 quake on Earth.

Lead author Jung-Hun Song of Imperial College London said:

What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction. The seismic waves tell us that there was a sideways sliding motion on a fault well below the surface, while the geology seen from orbit shows a region crossed by long-lived fault systems.

Song added:

What we see is that this is not just a ‘dead’ fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased.

Sadly, InSight lander ceased operations in 2022 due to too much dust accumulating on its solar panels. No active lander is currently recording new marsquakes on the surface of Mars. Perhaps we won’t discover the next marsquake until astronauts feel the red planet shake beneath them.

Bottom line: Researchers said the red planet is still tectonically active today. A team found the epicenter and cause of a marsquake at the Grand Canyon of Mars.

Source: Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris

Via Columbia University

item.title: Olbers’ paradox asks ‘Why is the night sky dark?’ - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Brian Jackson, Boise State University

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Why is space dark if the universe is filled with stars?

People have been asking why space is dark despite being filled with stars for so long that this question has a special name: Olbers’ paradox.

Astronomers estimate that there are about 200 billion trillion stars in the observable universe. And many of those stars are as bright or even brighter than our sun. So, why isn’t space filled with dazzling light?

I am an astronomer who studies stars and planets — including those outside our solar system — and their motion in space. The study of distant stars and planets helps astronomers like me understand why space is so dark.

You might guess it’s because a lot of the stars in the universe are very far away from Earth. Of course, it is true that the farther away a star is, the less bright it looks. A star 10 times farther away looks 100 times dimmer. But it turns out this isn’t the whole answer.

Imagine a bubble

Pretend, for a moment, that the universe is so old that the light from even the farthest stars has had time to reach Earth. In this imaginary scenario, all of the stars in the universe are not moving at all.

Picture a large bubble with Earth at the center. If the bubble were about 10 light-years across, it would contain about a dozen stars. Of course, at several light-years away, many of those stars would look pretty dim from Earth.

If you keep enlarging the bubble to 1,000 light-years across, then to one million light-years, and then one billion light-years, the farthest stars in the bubble will look even more faint. But there would also be more and more stars inside the bigger and bigger bubble, all of them contributing light. Even though the farthest stars look dimmer and dimmer, there would be a lot more of them, and the whole night sky should look very bright.

It seems I’m back where I started, but I’m actually a little closer to the answer.

Age matters in Olbers’ paradox

In the imaginary bubble illustration, I asked you to imagine that the stars are not moving and that the universe is very old. But the universe is “only” about 13 billion years old.

Even though that’s an amazingly long time in human terms, it’s short in astronomical terms. It’s short enough that the light from stars more distant than about 13 billion light-years hasn’t actually reached Earth yet. And so the actual bubble around Earth that contains all the stars we can see only extends out to about 13 billion light-years from Earth.

There just are not enough stars in the bubble to fill every line of sight. Of course, if you look in some directions in the sky, you can see stars. If you look at other bits of the sky, you can’t see any stars. And that’s because, in those dark spots, the stars that could block your line of sight are so far away their light hasn’t reached Earth yet. As time passes, light from these more and more distant stars will have time to reach us.

The Doppler shift and Olbers’ paradox

You might ask whether the night sky will eventually light up completely. But that brings me back to the other thing I told you to imagine: that all of the stars are not moving. The universe is actually expanding, with the most distant galaxies moving away from Earth at nearly the speed of light.

Because the galaxies are moving away so fast, the light from their stars is pushed into colors the human eye can’t see. This effect is the Doppler shift. So, even if it had enough time to reach you, you still couldn’t see the light from the most distant stars with your eyes. And the night sky would not be completely lit up.

If you wait even longer, eventually the stars will all burn out. Stars like the sun last only about 10 billion years. Astronomers hypothesize that in the distant future — a thousand trillion years from now — the universe will go dark, inhabited by only stellar remnants like white dwarfs and black holes.

Even though our night sky isn’t completely filled with stars, we live in a very special time in the universe’s life, when we’re lucky enough to enjoy a rich and complex night sky, filled with light and dark.

Brian Jackson, Associate Professor of Astronomy, Boise State University

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Bottom line: Olbers’ paradox asks why is space dark if the universe is filled with stars. The answer is that not all of the light from distant stars has reached us yet. Plus, the universe is expanding, so stars’ light gets red-shifted, pushing it into colors where our human eyes can’t see.

item.title: Why does anything exist? New theory emerges - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Why does anything exist?

Why does anything exist? And why is there something instead of nothing? The prevailing theory of how the universe began is the Big Bang theory. It states that some 13.8 billion years ago, a burst of growth created matter, space and time. And the Big Bang created not only matter, but antimatter.

Matter and antimatter destroy each other when they meet, releasing energy. If the early universe contained equal amounts of both, they should have wiped each other out, leaving behind a universe filled with energy but no stars, planets or people.

But on October 20, 2026, physicists from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said they have a new theory to why everything — including us — exists. They said an often-forgotten particle, the decoupled heavy neutrino, might explain how matter dominated in the early universe.

Co-author Rishav Roshan from the University of Southampton said:

This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed paper in the journal Physical Review Letters on September 8, 2026.

What is a decoupled heavy neutrino?

Neutrinos are tiny subatomic particles with no electric charge and almost no mass. They rarely interact with other matter. Trillions of them pass through your body every second without you noticing. Scientists sometimes call them ghost particles because they are so difficult to detect.

A decoupled heavy neutrino is a theoretical particle that’s incredibly massive with a slow decay. It’s called right-handed because its quantum spin aligns with its direction of motion. It would interact only weakly with other particles, so it could have survived for a long time in the early universe.

And because this particle would have lasted longer than other particles, it could have taken over the energy density of the cooling early universe. This would have allowed it to shift the balance to a matter-dominated universe.

Let’s go back to the beginning

In the moments after the Big Bang, the universe was extremely hot and dense. As it expanded, it cooled, allowing particles to interact and gradually form the building blocks of the universe we know today.

The researchers propose that the heavy neutrino could have lived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe’s energy. This would have changed how quickly the universe expanded and how its temperature evolved.

Roshan said:

The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles — like electrons and other leptons — interacted with their antiparticles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up.

A new look at the earliest universe

The researchers said the decoupled heavy neutrino could have profoundly altered the universe’s expansion history. Besides matter and antimatter interactions, they said these special neutrinos also could have had an impact on the production of dark matter and the generation of primordial gravitational waves.

Co-author Sudipta Show from the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said:

It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang.

So does this answer the question of why does anything exist? For now, it’s an intriguing theory but not a definitive answer. But it might bring us a step closer to understanding why the universe contains something rather than nothing.

Bottom line: Why does anything exist? A new theory by physicists suggests a forgotten particle, the decoupled heavy neutrino, might have shifted the balance between matter and antimatter.

item.title: Lucy mission to Trojan asteroids: 5 years of discoveries - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• NASA’s Lucy mission is headed to the Trojan asteroids. These asteroids, traveling ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit, have never been explored before.
  • Lucy is now less than a year away from the Trojans. But it has already made several exciting discoveries.
  • These include new findings at other asteroids in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

5 years into the Lucy mission

NASA’s Lucy spacecraft is getting ever closer to its destination, the Trojan asteroids. These are two groups of asteroids that travel ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit. Lucy is now less than a year away from meeting its first Trojan. Exciting!

Launched on October 16, 2021, Lucy has been traveling for about five years now. But even though it hasn’t reached the asteroids yet, it has already made several remarkable discoveries, researchers from the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) said on October 19, 2026.

An ambitious mission to unexplored asteroids

Lucy will be the first mission to explore the Trojan asteroids. Hal Levison at SwRI is the principal investigator of the mission. He said:

Lucy is an ambitious NASA mission, with plans to visit 11 asteroids in its 12-year mission to tour the Trojan asteroids that are located in two swarms leading and trailing Jupiter. As we passed through the main asteroid belt, we visited three asteroids, capturing close-up views of those bodies while performing engineering tests of the spacecraft’s innovative navigation system in advance of the main event to study the Trojans. These relics are effectively fossils of the planet formation process, holding vital clues to deciphering the history of our solar system.

Dinkinesh has a moon

Even though Lucy hasn’t reached the Trojans yet, it has already made several discoveries.

The first was at the asteroid Dinkinesh. Back in 2022, the mission team found that Lucy would come close to the asteroid, which was still unnamed at the time. Dinkinesh is in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

The flyby happened in November 2023. The mission team tweaked the spacecraft’s trajectory so it would fly even closer to Dinkinesh. And there was a surprise waiting for them.

The asteroid had a tiny moon! So now, scientists count that as being two asteroids. But there was yet another surprise.

The little moon, now named Selam, was a contact binary. That is, it had two parts that were joined together. So there were three bodies altogether, not just one.

Peanut-shaped Donaldjohanson

Later, in 2025, Lucy flew past another asteroid, Donaldjohanson. And this time, it was the asteroid itself that was a contact binary.

Donaldjohanson is peanut-shaped, with two large lobes joined together by a smooth “neck.” Simone Marchi, deputy principal investigator for Lucy, said:

The Donaldjohanson flyby revealed many surprises about the small asteroid. For instance, the peanut-shaped, two-lobed structure is connected by a remarkably smooth neck. The asteroid also wobbles, rotating end-over-end once every 10.5 Earth days while rolling around its lateral axis once every 26.5 days.

Gravity assists boot Lucy’s speed

During its journey, Lucy looped back and passed by Earth twice. Why? It might sound counterproductive, but the spacecraft uses Earth’s gravity to gain speed and fine-tune its trajectory.

The first gravity assist was in October 2022. Lucy passed only 220 miles (350 km) above the surface of Earth. This propelled Lucy into a two-year solar orbit. Lucy took images of Earth and the moon to calibrate its instruments.

Later, in December 2024, the second flyby increased its speed relative to the sun by over 16,000 mph (25,750 km/h). That put Lucy on a current path to make its first Trojan encounter in August 2027.

Lucy will make yet another Earth flyby in December 2030. It will then reach the second Trojan swarm of asteroids in March 2033.

When problems arise

With any mission, there can be problems that occur, and Lucy was no exception. Soon after launch, one of its two huge solar panels didn’t deploy properly.

However, mission engineers were able to diagnose the problem and get the solar panel to deploy far enough to save the mission.

Other observations

Lucy has been fortunate to witness some other events too during its journey.

In September 2022, NASA DART probe impacted the near-Earth asteroid Didymos (on purpose, to demonstrate planetary defense technology). And Lucy saw it happen.

In September 2025, Lucy observed the now-famous interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS as it passed through our solar system. 

But there is much more to come, as Levison noted:

Despite these eventful five years, most of Lucy’s mission still lies ahead. The main events start in less than a year as Lucy gets a close-up look at four Trojan asteroid systems: Eurybates and its satellite Queta in August 2027, Polymele and its as-yet-unnamed satellite in September 2027, Leucus in April 2028 and Orus in November 2028.

It will be exciting when Lucy finally reaches the Trojans. None of them have been seen up close before, so what will Lucy find?

Bottom line: NASA’s Lucy mission is now less than a year from reaching the Trojan asteroids near Jupiter. And it has already made some exciting discoveries along the way.
